SIR, Eaft India Houfe, 2d November 1807. 


I wave been honoured with yours of the 26th ult. ftating that you have “ received the 
« commands of the Right Honourable the Lords Commiffioners of His Majefty’s Treafury, to 
“ fuggeft the Jateft period at which it would be practicable to wind upthe Accounts depending 
«© between the Public and the Eaft India Company, either by the end of this year or the beginning 
“of next; that you are unable to yield obedience to thofe commands, without a reference to me on 
“ the fubjeét ;” defiring, therefore, * fuch obfervations from me as may affift you in replying to 
“ their Lordfhips’ dire&tions ;” and “ my opinion, as to the period within which it may probably 
“be praéticable to wind up the whole of the accaunts as they now ftand,”” 

In reply, I have to obferve, that it is not pofiible, in my opinion, to wind up the accounts 
either by the end of this year or the beginning of next, and for the following reafons: 

> aft. From the want of the-complete accounts from India of the charges of the Egyptian Expe- 
dition, as I have underftood from you, in the courfe of the examination we have been inaking, that 
you are not fatisfied with the corre€tnefs of the documents from which thofe charges have been 
tated; and I have no hefitation in acknowledging they are not fufficiently perfect to authorize 
your admiffion of them : before, therefore, this article of the Corapany’s claims can be clearly and 
explicitly ftated, it will be neceflary to wait the arrival of more particular information from 
India, . 

2dly. From the want of ftatements from His Majefty’s Pay Office, relative to the demands on. 
the Company for expences of the King’s Regiments ferving in India, you are aware, that thefe 
demands, as hitherto received, include only to the end of the year 1803, and the particular 
explanations of the accounts to that period, fo long ago and fo repeatedly defired, have not yet been 
furnithed. 

3dly. From want of more precife explanations regarding fome of the heads of charges againft 
the Public, contained in the laft abftra&t account, with a copy’ of which you have been furnithed ; 
viz, the expences of the lait Expedition to the Cape, thofe relative to Trinidad and Buenos 
Ayres. 

"and, laftly, From the difference of opinion which prevails, as to the conftru@tion of the prin- 
ciples intended to be laid down by the Committee of the Houfe of Commons, in their Report of 
June 1805, for tating the accounts of Ceylon and the Eaftern Iflands. From the communications 
I have been honoured with, I apprehend it is not likely that the Company will be contented to 
abide by the decifion of the Right Honourable the Lords Commiffioners of His Majefty’s Trea- 
fury, contained in their Lordfhips’ Minute of the 12th June laft, on the reference you found 
yourfelf under the neceffity of making to them upon this fubject, Until, therefore, fome accom- 
modation of this difagreement fhall take place, the final fettlement of the accounts muft be 
poftponed. 

‘Thefe are the principal obftacles which prefent themfelves to the completion of the accounts, 
at either of the periods you have mentioned; and from what is above ftated, you will readily per- 
ceive that it is entirely out of my power to offer an opinion, as to the period within which it may 
be praéticable to wind up the whole of the accounts as they now ftand,

Extra&t of TREASURY MINUTE, dated 14th December 1807 


Reap Letter from Mr. Wittwer, dated 4th November laft, in anfwer to one from this Board, 
relative to the probable period at which it will be praéticable to wind up the Accounts between the 
Public and the Eaft India Company, and enclofing copy of the correfpondence between him and 
Mr. Wright, the Officer appointed by the Eaft India Company to prepare the accounts. 

My Lords are of opinion, notwithftanding the feveral difficulties ftated by Mr. Wittwer and Mr. 
‘Wright, owing to fome of the accounts not being as yet received from India, and to that of the 
Pay Office not being completely made out, that it would be very defirable to balance the Account 
between the Public and the Eaft India Company, as well as it can be done, from the materials and 
vouchers which now exift, or which may very {peedily be brought forward, and put into the 
hands of the refpeétive Accountants, up to the end of the year 1803, which My Lords con- 
ceive will include all claims on either fide, up to the clofe of the laft war: And My Lords are 
therefore pleafed to dire&t, that the Accountants, having reference to the principles laid down in 
the Reports of the Committees of the Houfe of Commons, and in the Minute of this Board of 
1ath June laft, fhould proceed to prepare fuch an account, and to ftrike the balance thereupon, fo 
that it may, if poffible, be fubmitted to their Lordfhips early in the enfuing feffion of Parliament. 

In direéting this account fo to be prepared and balanced, My Lords are of opinion, that, notwith- 
ftanding any balance which may be declared to be duc on either fide, it fhall be open to either 
party to produce fuch claims, though arifing prior to the end of the year 1803 ; and that fuch claims 
fhould be admitted, if properly fupported by proofs and vouchers to the fatistaétion of the other; 
and, in like manner, that either party may, upon what n:ay appear to him fufficient grounds (if 
furnifhed to him by any information or documents obtaincd fubfequent to the account being fo 
balanced) proceed to challenge and difallow any items therein, and claim, upon a ftatement of the 
cafe, to have fuch particular heads of charge reconfidered. And My Lords are further of opinion, 
that any fettlement of accounts that may take place between the Public and the Eaft India Com- 
pany, upon the principles, and with the exceptions hercin ftated, ought not to preclude the re- 
{pective Accountants from proceeding to examine and baance the accounts fubfequent to the 
year 1803, as expeditioufly as the nature of the refpective ciaims, and of the vouchers by which 
they may be fupported, will admit; but that this latter acccunt fhould be proceeded upon feparately, 
and kept diftinét from the former.

difcharge of fuch part of the military expenfes which may have been incurred under

Your Committee, however, deem it proper to observe, in regard to tlis Result, 
that it is drawn from the Documents referred to in their original fiate, and thr it 
may be subject to some alteration, as well by a minute analysis of the Documents 
themselves, as by other adjuftments which your Committee feel it incumbent on 
them not to omit mentioning ; and upon these it may not be improper to offer a few 
explanatory observations. 

The Consignments of Goods and Stores are credited in the Indian Books, at the full 
amount charged in the Invoices; which amount includes an addition of 10 per 
cent. on the original coft; while the amount of Bills is credited at a rate of Exchange 
producing less considerably than the amount paid in England. 

How far all the sums ftated under the head of Territorial Payments from the 
Company's Treasury in England are accurately described, may admit of quettion ; 
Your Committee, however, think a large proportion are fairly described by 
that title. 

The Commercial Concern has not been debited for the Charge of Prince of Wales 
Island, or Bencoolen, which has been defrayed from the Territorial Revenue. 

The amount of the Losses of Consignments, by capture and fhipwreck, has been 
extensive; Outward £. 335,893; homeward £. 1,027,209; together £. 1,363,102. 
The Commercial Concern is debited by India for the whole'of the Consignments 
homeward, and has not received Credit for the full amount of those outward, 
A doubt may arise how the Joss so incurred is to he charged, whether to the Teii- 
toriés or to the Commerce. . 

‘The Advances in India.chargeable to His Mojefiy’s Government, and ‘the Dise 
bursements by the Paymafters General, are not carried down to so late a period as 
moft of the other items. 

Subject to these qualifications, the inferences suggefted by the Result firft thewn, 
the correctness of the prineiples-on which it is drawn, together with the adjuftments 
adyerted to, Your Committee humbly submit to the judgment of The House.

Examination of WILLIAM WRIGHT, Esq. Auditor of Indian Accounts, 


A® E you Auditor of Indian Accounts ?——Yes. 
Is it the duty of your office to draw up the Accounts of Revenues and Charges, and of 
the Debts and Assets of the Company in India ?—Itis. 

Are the Statements in the Annual Budget Accounts, termed Abftrat Receipts and Dis- 
bursements of Bengal, Madras and Bombay respeétively, Abftraéts made of Statements in 
detail received from those Presidencies ?—They are. - 

Do not the Statements so received purport to be in general the entire Cash Transactions of 
those Presidencies, comprizing the Revenues and Charges as well as the Extraordinary Re- 
ceipts and Disbursements ? rainly. 

Do they not form the basis of the Accounts drawn by you, thewing diftinétly the Revenues 
and Charges of those Presidencies under their respestive heads ?—They do. 

Has it not occurred both in Receipt and Disbursement, that articles included under the 
head Extraordinary in the Statements received from India, have been considered as Revenue 
or Charge, and carried to account as such ia the Accounts to which the laft queftion 
refers ?—Certainly. vee : 

Has it not occurred, with regard to the Bengal Accounts particularly, that the Military 
Charge has been calculated on the Advances made to the Paymafters, because the detailed 
Disbursements had not been received in time for completing the Accounts ?—It has. 

Ta such cases, as well as others, when Documents are afterwards received from India, 
which render it necessary to make alterations in Accounts presented to Parliament, are you 
aotin.the habit of so deing?—Conftantly. % 

Are not Books kept at the several Presidencies, termed General Books ?—Yes, 

Are not the General Books supposed to include, in Abftraét at leaft, the whole of the 
‘Financial Transaétions of those Presidencies ?—Unqueftionably. ; 

Are the Statements of Receipt and Disbursement firft alluded to, supposed-to be drawn ig 
conformity with the General Books ?—They are. 

Are you in the habit, as occasion may require, of examining the connexion between the 
General Books and those Statements, and of adjufting the Accounts accordingly i—Yes.

Par. 1—IN a former dispatch we gave you dire@ions for the liquidation of the Debts 
owing by the Rajah of Tanjore to his privaie creditors ; at the same tine we intimated our 
intention to take into our consideration the more considerable claims of the Crediturs of the 
Nabob of Arcot; and we uow transmit to you our directions on this subject. 


2. As the Debt to the Crecitors in the Cavalry Loan is already discharged, our present 
directions extend only to the claims of the Creditors in the Consolidated Debt of 1777. 


3. As the Compan: , under the conditions of the treaty of 1787, found it necessary, in 
order to provide for the defence of the country, to take possession of the Nabob’s territories, 
and to apply the revenues arising from them to the expense of the war, and uot to the 
payment of the sums which, if peace had continued, would have become annually due to 
nis Highness’s private Creditors, according to the arrangements dire@ed by the Court’s 
Orders of December 1784; the Company are to be considered as having borrowed the sums 
which would have been payable to the, Creditors, if the Nubob had fulfilled his engagements 
prior to the treaty of peace made by Lord Cornwallis, which money is to be accounted tor 
agreeable to the arrangement above mentioned, Those suins appear to be as follow: Firtt, 
the Lutereft on Pagodas 54,98,300. The Principal due to those Creditors at six per cent. for 
two years, from Auguft 1788 to Auguft 1790, being Pagodas 6,59,820; which Lntereft is the 
thare of the twelve lacs of Pagodas per annum, which they were entitled to receive by the 
Orders in our said Letter of g* December 1784, until the Cavalry Loan thould be discharged ; 
but, # it (hall appear that the Creditors of 1777 have received a proportion of the sums paid 
by the Nabob, on account of those two years, such proportion is to be dedu&ted. Secondly, 
As the Cavalry Loan would, if the payments to the Creditors had been duly made, have been 
discharged before _31*t of Augatt 1790, five lacs of Pagodas became annually due to the 
Creditors in the Debt of 1777, which for two years, from that date to the date of Lord 
Cornwallis’s treaty made in July 1792, amounts to Pagodas 10,00,000, naking together 
Pagodas 16,59,820. On this sum, or such amount as fhali be found due on these principles, 
intereft at six per cent. fhall be allowed to the Creditors irom Auguft 1792, being the month 
after Lord Cornwallis’s treaty was made ; which Intereft on the above sum amounts to Pago- 
das 1,99,198 for two years to the 31° of Auguft 1794; making together Pagodas 18,59,018. 
This sum or such other amount as shall, on the principles here laid down, be found due to 
the Creditors, we direét that your Government fhall discharge, either by cath, or by notes 
bearing six per cent. Intereft from 31‘ Auguft 1794, payable only at Madras; but in the 
latter alternative, the Creditors are to take the notes at the current premiuin or discount. 
But in order to prevent the inconvenience which might arise from so large a quantity of 
notes being issued immediately, we direct that they be issued progressively in such propor 
tions as to prevent the market from being overftocked, and the value of your notes in ge- 
neral thereby reduced from bearing a premiom to be issued at a discount. 


4. To prevent our Orders on this subjeét irom being misunderfiood, we send a Statement 
(No. 1.) containing the Debts which we suppose will Tae been found due by the Company 
to the Creditors on 31't Augutt 1794, in the Consolidated Debt, according to the arrange- 
ments we have mentioned; and a Statement (No. 2.) fhewing the amount of what will re= 
main due by the Nabob to those Creditors after the notes we have mentioned thall be given, 
and after the kifts for two vears payable by the Nabob, according to Lord Cornwullis’s treaty, 
Ahall have been paid to them, 


5. We also dire@, that as the payments which the Nabob was bound to make in every 
year to his Creditors have been, for the accommodation of his Highness, reduced from 
72 lacs of Pagodas, to 6,21,105 Pagodas; the payment of the said 6,21,105 Pagodas to the 
Creditors in the Consolidated Debt of 1777 thall not henceforth be suspended on any 
account whatever, but {hall be regularly made to those Creditors, until the Debt due to them, 
with Lnterelé at 6 per cent, frail be fully paid,

Para. 4. AS by the 7 Article of the Treaty with the Rajab of Tanjore of the 10 April 
1787, (which fiipulates that, in the event of war, four-fifths of the Revenues of the Tanjore 
country, (hall be annually appropriated to the military expenses) all payments on account of 
the Rajah’s private Creditors virtually ceased on the commencement of hottilities ; so by the 
10% article, which flipulates that the said annual four-fifths of the Tanjore Revenues, fhall, 
afler the term ion of the war, continue to be applied to the discharge of all debts and 
expenses that may be incurred or arise during the course of the war, until the Rajah’s pro- 
portion of one-fifth of the whole expense is discharged, the private Creditors are not entitled 
to any payment till such proportion thail be completely liquidated. 


&. The dividends hitherto made to the Tanjore Creditors have been improperly calcu- 
lcted in the proportion that the a:mual Intereit due to them bore to the actual Receipt; we 
therefore think it necessary to lay dewn a rule for your future guidance, whenever the 
period fhall arrive for putting the Rajah a; into possession of bis country, upon all 
“arrears of Subsidy being discharged, and his proportion of the expenses incurred in the war 
completely liquidated ; viz. 


The full amount of the Subsidy, agreeably to the kifts mentioned in the treaty, muft in the 
firft inftance be secured to the Company. As the Company are to provide for the general 
defence of the country, aud as the Hiaja's roportion of the military expenses has been 
settled on a fair caiculation, this is indisputable. 


After the amount of the anoual Subsidy fhall have been thus previously secured to the 
Company, agreeably to the fiipulations in the 2¢ article ef the treaty, the Creditors thall 
receive’ their proportion of the sums that may be paid to the Company under the 14" ar- 
ticle. But as the Company, since the conclusion of the treaty of 1787, have, for a valuable 
consideration, obisined aright to the annua! Peishcufh usually paid by the Rajah to the 
Nabob of Arcot; and also to the lage arrear that was due thereon, and have in consequence, 
in order to afford relief to the Rajeh’s finances, consented to make for the present a very 
cons‘derabie reduction in the sams to bé annually paid by the Rajzh on those accounts, 
agrecably to the ftipulations in the 14" article, you are to observe, that fhouid the Rajab’s

Para. 6. THE Governor General laid before us a Letter from ccountant General, sug-

of the Company io India. 


7. Lor raising a Fund for the liquidation of the exifting Debt, which amounted at the 
end of December daft to about six crores and fifty lacs of Sicca Rupees, it is proposed, that 
‘Bills thall be drawn upon you quarterly for S* K* 325,000 or 13 lacs of S* R* per annum 
(being equal to 2 per cent. on the whole Debt, until the extinction of the Debt, which, 
according to the calculation in the Accountant General’s letter, will be effected in about 
twenty years. 


8. The liquidation of any future annual addition to the present Debt, is to be provided for 
in the same manner. 


9. Although the Plan may not be produttive of all the advantages ftated in Mr. Myer’s. 
Teter, we are satisfied, that besides providing for the discharge of your Debts in the moft 
advantageous manner, it will contribute por to uphold the value of public securities, 
especially at periods when the exigencies of Government may render it necessary for them 
to avail themselves of their credit to a considerable extent; and consequently that we thall 
be enabled to raise Supplies, not only to a larger amount, but on terms more favourable than 
has hitherto been practicable, without, at the same time, occasioning that great depreciation 
of the public securities which had hitherto invariably followed every extraordinary demand 
on our resources, and which in its operation has been equally injurious to your interefis, and 
to those of the great body of the holders of your securities. 


10, For the details of the Plan, we beg to refer you to the Accountant's letter. We fhall 
here only add, that from the considerations above flated, and being of opinion that the Plan 
did not, in any respect, interfere with the engagements between Government and its present 
Creditors, we resolved to adopt it, and the Accountant General has been called upon to lay 
before us a Draft of the Rules for the application and management of the Fund.

The Serecr Commirrex appointed to enquire into the presen 
State of the Affairs of The East India Company, and to report the 
same, as it shall appear to thém, to the House, with their 
Observations thereupon ; and also, their Proceedings from time 
to time to. the House ;. Have, pursuant to the Orders of 
the House, further examined the Matters to them referred ; and 
have agreed upon the following REPORT: 


yor Committee, in their Second and Third Reports, have submitted to the 
House the results of their enquiry into the State of the Affairs of the East 
‘India Company, as far as related to the Receipt and Expenditure of the Treasuries 
‘of the several Presidencies and Settlements in India, during seventeen years, from 
1792-3 to 1808-9 inclusive; and having stated the Ordinary and Extraordinary 
Funds, with the sources from which they were respectively derived, together with the 
application of them, have cndeavoured, in the latter of the above Reports, to shew, 
the general effect produced upon the Balance in India by the various and compli- 
-cated transactions which had been the objects of their detailed exaniination. 


Your Committee anxiously desired to pursue the course of enquiry proposed in 
their Third Report, and complete the investigation of the State of the Finances ge- 
erally, both abroad and at home, during the fast Session of Partiament; but found 
the time insufficient to cnable them to enter so fully into the Financial transactions 
termed those of the [ume Concern, as the importance of the subject rendered in- 
dispensable, notwithstanding the Accounts and Documents connected with. it were 
neither so numerous, nor apparently so complicated, as those which had already been 
brought to the notice of the House. 


Your Committee having already described generally the nature of these Accounts, 
and stated their intention of considering the China ‘Trade, and the Expense of the 
Settlement of the Island of St. Helena in connection with them, now proceed to re- 
‘view these branches of the Company’s Affairs. 


The Home Accounts commence in 1793, and end in 1$10; those of ‘China and 
‘St. Helena in 1792, and terminate in 1809, embracing respectively, like these of 
India, the space of seventeen years. 

The House is already apprized, that although the transactions of the Treasury at 
home are in their cha’ Y ipally Commercial, they are nevertheless clesely in- 
terwoven with others of a Political nature, and that to a degree which yenders the 
Cifficulty of distinct separaticn much greater than has been experienced in the cxa~ 
amination of the Aeccunts confined to the Affairs in India, The manner in which

the Rooks have been kept in the latter case, enabled your Committee to make some 
distinction, and to offer such Statements and Results as they trust will have fur- 
nished the means of assisting the judgement of the House in distinguishing the Poli- 
tical transactions from those more sti ctiy Commercial; but in the Home Accounts, 
the entire Receipt and | penditure in cach year is compressed into one gene- 
mal Cash Account, in which, as to the Disbursements particulerly, what is Political, 

v blended toa considerable amount with what is apparently a Charge 
mmercial. ‘This Account has been presented annually to Parliament, 
under the ions of the Act of 1793, accompanied by the Statement of the 
Debits and 3 of the Company at home. Other Accounts have been also pre- 
sented to the Hense (as that entitled the Stock by Computation and the Amount of 
the Sales of Goods in cach year) on distinct motions for the same. These several 
Accounts will form the basis of the investigation proposed to be pursued; but Your 
Comittee will, us occasion nay prescribe, add'to their Appendix such further State- 
ments as shall appear r ite lly to elucidate the subject, and enable them to 
bring the wile to the view of the House in the most intelligible manner. It will 
not be in the power of Your Coumittee to adhere precisely to the course they have 
pursucd in respect to the Indian Accomnts; as upon many occasions recourse must 
be had to e: » for the exhibition of certain results; but in every case the grounds 
of the calculations will be distinctly explained, that the House may judge of the cor- 
s of the principles upon which they are made. 

Itis not however meant by this remark to queftion the propriety of the mode in 
ich the Books of the Company at Home have been kept, or to imply that the 
Accounts piesented annnally to the House unter the directions of the Act, are not 
of a deseription to tuvnish the information intended by the Legistature. « Your Com- 
mittee, on ‘the ec er it due to the Court of Directors to state, that with 
respect to this branch of the Accounts, which is under their more immediate control, 

the | provisions of the Act have been most punctually attended to, both as to the mode 
of Statement (which is upon a very general principle) and the time. The Accounts in 
question appear to have been pr epared i in strict conformity to the system under which 
the Coinpany’s '3 affairs have been ‘conducted, of combined Political and Commercial 
management, the separation of which has not been hitherto required.

The Concern in Crna being the most import tant branch of the Commerce of the 
Company, Your Committee will examine the employment of Frnds in that ‘Trade, 
hefure they review the effects produced by it upon the Home Treasury. ‘Phe Ex- 
peuses of the Settlement of the Island of St. Helena, which are principally defrayed 
by Supplies from. England, will be next considered. By this process the enquiry into 
the state of the Company's Affairs abroad will have preceded that of the Home 
‘Treasury, and by a gradual course the combination of the whole, as originally pro-

‘The connection-of the Company with China is entirely ‘of a Commercis! nature, 
and although any lenathened explanation of the principles upon which this highly 
imports at branch of th ‘cmmercial economy is conducted inay be superfluous, 
ar nature of it presctibes the propricty of offering some general remarks 
uation of the Liouse. 

‘Trade witly China has for a very long period formed a part of the exclusive 

yy ge of, the Company, and has been carried: on upon principles conducive, in a 
very ctuinent degree, not only to the advantage of those embarked in it, but likewise 
terests of the British Empire in its Revenue, in the emp! loyment of its 
re dina steady end continned demand for its Manufactures. It is never- 
jess fact universally known, that the Company have no footing whatever in 
China coming under the denomination of permanent; that the intercourse with the 
Merchants of that extensive Empire is very limited, being exclusively confined to a 
sinall Pactory.in the vicinity of the City of Canton, occupied by the sufferance of the 
Court of Pekin, under strict regulations, designating the parties with whom, andthe 
‘manner in which the Trade is to be conducted. ‘The Fu ‘actory of Canton may there: 
fore be considered as the place of mere occasional residence for the convenience o| 
the Agents of the Company in their transactions with the Merchants, ‘who are termed 
Hong) ferchants, expressly licensed by the Chinese Government to have dealings with 
them. These MM Merchants re very limited in number, being in 1793 twelve, and 


The 


-in 180$ fourteen. 


Affairs of The EAST INDIA COMPANY, 419 


The official designation of the Agents of the Company is that of Supra-Cargoes. 

‘hey are united in one Commission, aud gencrally the four Senior are termed the 
President and Select Committee, who are assisted in the transaction of the busi- 
ness of the Factory by the remainder, and by Writers and others holding sub- 
ordinate appointments, the whole being under special covenants for the periormance 
of the duties committed to them respectively. A description of the several persons 
thus employed is added to the Appendix. ‘I'he residence of the Supra-Cargoes and 
their Assistants at the Factory is only during the season of their intercourse with the 
Chinese Merchants, for receiving and paying for the produce of the Country. The 
purchases of this produce used to bein part made by the barter of the Woollens 
and Metals consigned from England, and in part by Cash. But for some years this 
plan has been altered, and an absolute sale has been made of the Exports of this 
Country, the produce of which, combined with the other Funds of the Canton Trea~ 
-sury, is applied to the discharge of the demands ofthe Merchants of China, for the 
goods supplied by them. 


The business of the Season being finished, and the ships laden and dispatched on 
their return to England, the Supra-Cargoes retire from .the Mactory to the Island 
of Macao, a Settlement belonging to the Portuguese, where. they continue till the 
opening of the ensuing Season. The periods of the commencement and close of the 
‘Season are. not distinctly laid down, being affected by various contingencies; and as 
to what is termed the official year according to the books of the Factory, Your 
Committee find that no precise period has ever been fixed for its definition; but the 
balancing of them has generally been governed by the conclusion of the Season, which 
has been most communly in the months of February or March. ‘The species of 
Coin made “use of in the books of the Factory, are Tales, Mace, and Candarines, 
which are nominal. The common valuation of the Tale being at 6s, 8d. Sterling, 
will be assumed in the sequel of this Report. 


The produce of the Chinese Empire, immediately the object of the trade of the 
Company, consists at present only of ‘I'cas, Silk, and Nankeens. In former years 
China-ware was purchased to a considerable amount, but was relinquished in conse- 
quence of the improvement of the British manufacture, which has superseded the 
necessity of the.importation of that of China. 


The extent of this branch of the Company’s Commerce, with the result of it, and 
-the Funds by which it has been carried on, will be brought into view in other parts of 
this Report. Your Committee will therefore only add in this place, that.a consider- 
able part of those Funds was produced by Exports from this Country in Woollens and 
Metals, carried to the utmost extent that, from: the best information, it was conccived 
.the market.in China would.admit. ~ :

adverted to, is uniformly added to the Invoice Price of the goods. There is, however, 
a further apparent Expenditure not included, which comes under the denomination 
of Loss, which will hereatter be more distinctly noticed.

The proprietary possession of the Island of Sr. Herena, the expense of which is 
next to be considered, has from a distant period been vested in the East India Com- 
pany. In the’ reign of Charles IL it was granted as a port of refreshment for 
ships engaged in the India ‘Trade, on their homeward-bound voyage, and transferred 
to the present United Company on their first incorporation. 

An Account of the Revenues of the Island, and the Charges incurred in its main-" 
tenanee and defence, was annually laid before Parliament_in the same manner as 
those of the other possessions of the Company. Your Committee being informed 


‘that some of those Accounts required correction, have called for an amended Account, 


shewing the Revenues and Charges during the seventcen years, from 1792-3 to 
3808-9. This, Account is inserted in the Appendix. It should however be here 
observed, that the books of this Island are closed on the goth September in each 
year. According to this Account, the Civil Charges amounted to £. 236,369, the 
Military to £.772,637, and the expense of Buildings and Fortifications to £.71,908 ; 
making a total gross Charge of £. 1,080,914. The Revenues of the Island, arising 
from Reots, Farms, or Licenses, for the exclusive privilege of dealing in particular 
articles of consumption, and Customs, amounted to £. 14,256 ; so that the nct Charge 
of the Island during this period was £. 1,060,058. 

The importance of this Settlement has occasioned the necessity of particular atten- 
ticn to its security, the effect of which, in increased Charge, is apparent on the view. 
of the Statement now referred to, especially in the Military Expenses, and in the For- 
tifications. The increase of Charge is likewise to be attributed to additions made to 
the personal allowances of both the Civil and Military Servants of the Company. ‘The 
net Expense of the year 1792-3, previous to the War, was £.33,850, and it increased 
almost progressively till the year 1807-8, when the Amount was £. 102,437. In the 
next year it fell to £.83,150. On the average of the whole period, the net Charge’ 
amounted to £.62,744. But Your Committee having likewise enquired whether any’ 
further expense may not have been incurred in addition to what has been already! 
stated, find that on the transactions more immediately Commercial, as the sale and‘ 
issue of the various articles imported into the Island, a net Loss is stated on the books’ 
amounting to the sum of £.48,540. The Account shewing this Result is added to 
the Appendix, and exhibits the amount of Profits in the several years, at £.180,132, 
and the Losses at £. 228,672, producing the Result before stated. But the actual Loss 
is not tothis extent, because the Invoice price of the Consignments from Europe was,

Your Committee having shewn the nature and extent of the Trade of the Com- 
pany, will next proceed to the examination of the Result of it upon their Finances, 
or in other words of the Profit derived from it. ‘This point, in so far as the Trade 
from India is concerned, has led to such variety of opinions, and has been the 
subject of so much controversy amongst those whose general information on Com- 
mercial subjects and particular acquaintance with the Trade in question gives their 
opinions great authority, as to render any conclusion that may be offered a matter 
of considerable delicacy, it being hardly possible that any decision between the con- 
flicting parties should escape objection. 


It would be obviously hopeless to arrive at any determination respecting the Profit 
alluded to, from the Statements already the subject of discussion, as they ouly shew 
the Sales, the Receipts and the Payments made, with the Proceeds, as a simple 
Balance of Cash from year to year, according to the system upon which the Com- 

iny’s Concerns have been uniformly conducted; which, owing to its being so 
intimately involved with the affsirs of the Territories in India, cannot be properly 
termed a mere Commercial one. This circumstance necessarily imposed modes of 
arrangement and management most conducive to the interests of both. The com- 
bination of these interests having so repeatedly been brought to the notice of the 
House, Your Committee only here make a reference to it in order to justify the 
necessity of resorting to calculations upon Estimate, for the purpose of affording 
any intelligible view of the Result or Profit upon the Import Trade of the Company 
from India and China. 


Your Committee are fully aware of the objections that may be started to this 
mode of calculation, if it be contemplated on principles abstractedly Commercial, in 
as much as, upon. those principles, the Profit or Loss upon Commercial adventure, 
ought to be ascertained with strict precision; but they trust that the observations 
already made will explain why this is absolutely impracticable, and those observa~

themselves under the necessity of adopting, unless what in their judgment is a very

Tt may not however be improper t® remark, in more detailed: illustration of the 
necessity of having recourse to calculation by estimate, that the Shipping employed 
by the Company have, in conformity with their system, been for the most part, 
during a very long period, constructed for Warlike as well as Commercial service ; 
and have been frequently, and in fact constantly used for Political purposes, either 
in conveyance of Troops and Military Stores, or in Expeditions against the Posses- 
sions of the Enemy. The part ofthe Freight therefore chargeable to the Trade can 
only be ascertained by estimate. Further, a practice has prevailed, whether correct 
or not Your Committee do not pretend to determine, of charging the largest propor- 
tion of the whole Freight of the voyage to the homeward-bound trade, ‘The Charges 
also directly appertaining to the Trade are so interwoven with those of a Political 
nature, that it would be extremely difficult to make a separation ; it has been there- 
fore the practice to calculate a certain part of the General Charges in England as 
‘Commercial, assuming § per cent. on the Gross Sale Amount of the Goods as the 
fair proportion so chargeable. The difficulty of ascertaining the particular Fund 
from which the purchase of the Goods was made, might likewise be mentioned, 
from the effect which would be preduced upon the Invoice price of them in the rate 
of Exchange. 4 


From these several causes, but more particularly from those applying to the 
Freight and Charges, such difficulties have ever existed in the way of celculating the 
Profit or Loss on the Trade“upon actual Accounts, that the custom has obtained of 
shewing them-upon estimate. Estimates of this description have, on many occa- 
sions, been laid upon the Table of the House, and particularly on the renewal of 
the Company’s Charter in 1793. So late as the Session of 1810, the Court of 
Directors inserted in the Appendix to an Exposition of the state of the Company's 
Finances, a computation of the Profits upon the Trade, drawn upon similar prin- 
ciples. It must be remarked, however, that the Invoice price of the Goods, in the 
several doctments now adverted to, is calculated with reference to the Exchange 
on such part of the purchase as was made by Monies procured for Bills upon the 
Company in England. 

As the Result proposed to be shewn, canriot therefore be ascertained otherwise 
than upon estimate, the attention of Your Committee has been particularly directed to 
the principle to be observed in the framing of such Estimate. In respect to the 
Freight and Charges upon the goods, they do not at present see reason to depart from 
the course usually pursued ; but as regards the Invoice price of the goods, upon every 
consideration connected with the plan which has been laid down in the prescnt 
enquiry, and as applicable to the general combination proposed to be made of 
the Result of the Financial operations. abroad.and at home, itis desirable that the 
Disbursements from the several ‘Treasuries in India and China,. for the purchase of 
Goods, as shewn in the Invoice Amount of such as were brought to sale, should uni- 
forusly be converted into Sterling moncy at the same rate of exchange used in the 
several Accounts that have been hitherto the objects of examination. 


This mode of calculation Your Committee readily admit is liable to observation, 
and perhaps exception, because according to the rates of exchange thus used, an 
unfair view might be said to be given of the outlay of money in the purchase of the 

oods, in so far as those purchases were made by money raised by Bills upon the 
Company, in which case the real exchange at which the Lills were drawn and paid, 
should be the rate used in computing the ‘Invoice price. ‘The only method by which 
this objection is to be met, is by ascertaining the difference between the Amount of 
the Bills drawn, calculated at the rate now assumed, and the Amount actually paid. 
This difference would be a fair deduction from the Profit upon the Sales. As to 
China, the whole would be deducted; but as to India, considerable difficulties would. 
be in the way of distinguishing the Bills drawn for Commercial, from those drawn for 
Political purposes. 

These observations Your Committee trust will explain the obstacles which present 
theniselves in the way of this part of their enquiry, and evince the neccssity of 
estimate in order to furnish the information desired. ‘They have therefore added to 
the Appendix, an Estimate of the Profit upon the Trade from India and China 

respectively,

Bills, converiing the Foreign Coins into Sterling moncy at the exchanges used in the

The partial view already given of the Profits being purposely confined to their 
effect at home, the Disbursements in India termed Commercial Charges not added 
to the Invoices, amounting to £.2,916,279, have not been taken into the present 
calculation; they will however be brought to account hereafter. 


The nature of these Charges has been adverted to in the Third Report of Your Com- 
mittee; as well as the duties of the Boards of Trade, and the Officers under them at 
the several Presidencies, the Pay and Allowances of which Departments they include. 
It is clearly just that the largest proportion of the sum now stated, should be deemed 
a Charge upon the goods purchased in India under the superintendence of these De- 
partments, and from being in fact an addition to the Invoice cost of the goods, must 
tend, pro tanto, to diminish the Amount assumed as the Profit on the Trade; but the - 
difficulty of determining the sum that may be so charged to the goods exclusively, is 
great, if the general duties of the Boards of Trade is taken ‘into consideration. These 
duties, including the direction of the manufacture of Salt and Opium at Bengal, the 
Customs at that Presidency, and in part at Madras, cannot be considered as exclu- 
sively Commercial, independent of the consideration that the Marine Department, and 
the business of providing Shipping for Political purposes, are under its conduct. 


For a more detailed explanation of the various functions imposed on these 
Departments, Your Committee beg leave to call the particular attention of the 
House to a Statement delivered in by one of its Members, and inserted in the 
Appendix. , : : 


The examination of the detail of the Estimate from which the Result upon the 
Company’s Trade has been produced, renders some further explanation requisite; 
and first, in reference to the general connection of this Estimate with the Statement 
which has been before referred to, in order to shew the nature and extent of the 
Trade as exhibited by the gross produce of the Sales, that the difference between the 
produce thus stated, and the Amount in the Estimate, is in part to be ascribed to the 
effect of re-sales, and in part to the sale of Rice and Wheat not brought to account 
in the Estimate. : , 


The extent ofthe Trade from India and China has been shewn by the produce of 
the Sales of the goods from thence. ‘The extent of this Trade, according to the sum 
annually embarked in it, so as to produce this Sale Amount, is to be ascertained by 
reference to the Estimate now brought forward, by which the Prime Cost of the goods 
imported from India and brought to sale, appears'to be £. 23,060,334. ; adding the 
difference in the rate of Exchange £. 520,799, the Total is £. 23,581,133, and is the 
Amount employed during the seventeen years.in the purchase of goods from India, and 
brought to sale, being on an average £. 1,387,125. 


The Prime Cost of goods imported from China was, on the same principle, 
4, 27,157,066 ; difference in rate of Exchange £. 996,454; Total £. 28,153,500, 
which is onan average £. 1,656,088. 

The whole of the Amount so employed during the period, is £. 51,734,633, and 
shews the extent of the Trade upon this principle, trom whence it will re-uit that the 
anual Expenditure for the purchase of goods from India and China, as far as they 
have been brought to sale in England, was upon an average £. 3,043,214. 


It will be remarked that after tse year 1798-9 the Customs stated in the Estimate 
to have been paid upon the good: “mported from India, amount to much less than in 
former years. Your Committee having examined into the cause of this difference, 
find that it is not to be imputed to a positive defalcation in the Duties levied on the 
importation of goods from India, but to.an alteration in the mode of their payment, 
in consequence of an Act passed in the year 1799, iatituled, ““ An Act for permitting 
“ certain Goods imported from the East Indies to be warehoused, and for repealing 
“ the Duties now payable thereon, aud granting other Duties iv lieu thereof.” 


An explanation of the particular causes which led to the passing of this Act, is to 
be found in several documents already upon the Table of the House, which were 
presented end printed in. pursuance of their Orders of 12th, 15th and 18th June 
1801, ‘These documents comprize a Memorial from the Directors of the East 
India Company to the Lords of the Treasury, dated 7th May 1797, on the subject of 

reyguladng 


Affairs of The EAST INDIA COMPANY. acy 


regulating the Duties on East India Goods, with sundry Papers annexed ; 
Memorial of the Merchants and principal Agents in England for persons r r 
the Kast Indies, to the Lords of the ‘I'reasury, dated May 1797, sctting forth the 
advantages that would arise from lowering the Duties on East India CGroods; and 
another Memorial of the Merchants, Buyers of Goods at the Kast India Company, 
Sales for exportation, to the Lords of the Treasury, dated the 31st May 1797, 
tating their entire acquiescence in the reasonings contained in the Memorial of the 
Court of Directors. ‘The principal objects of the respective Memoriaiists appear to 
have heen the removal of some serious impediments to the effect intended to be pro- 
duced by the Regulating Act of 1793; by which removal such a facility would be 
afforded to the export ot India Goods to the Continent, as effectually to maintain a 
compeiition in the markets with Foreign ‘Traders. Circumstanced as the ‘Trade was, 
the purchaser of the goods at the Sales was obliged to employ a capital to the extent 
of the Sule price, including the Duties payable on them, a drawback being returned 
on their exportation. Some advantage was likewise expected to be derived as to the 
goods sold for home consumption. 


The proposition of the Court of Directors thus acquiesced in by all the parties 
interested in the Trade, was that all goods from India and China, except Tea, 
should be allowed to be imported and warchoused without being subject to any Duty 
till sold, and then to be subject only to a positive Duty of 2 per cent. on the Sale 

. Value, to be paid by the Company out of the Sale Price, and to remain with the Crown, 

whether the goods were exported or not. The goods taken out of the warehouse for 
home consumption to be subject to the amount then payable, a3 also to the 2 per 
cent. additipnal Duty. . 

Such were the general principles upon which the Act above adverted to was 

founded ; and the sum inserted in the column of Customs upon - the goods since the 
“time of passing the Act is to be considered as the Amount paid from the Company's 
‘Treasury upon those principles, exclusive of the Duty upon ‘Tea, but of course is not 
to be looked upon as the entire Revenue derived from the Company’s Trade, the 
remainder being paid by the purchasers on clearing the goods for home con- 
sumption. 

The principle upon which the Freight of .the goods is estimated has been already 
adverted to, it only now remains again to remark, that it is doubtful .whether it is 
perfectly correct to charge more Freight upon the Imports than actually belongs to 
them, because the accuracy of the Result, as applicable to them exclusively, is thereby 
questionable. 

The Charges being estimated at 5 per cent. on the Gross Sale Amount, as already 
stated, certainly bears the appearance of an arbitrary calculation, and in fact may be 
so considered. It should however be here observed, that from an anxiety to ascer- 
tain how far the calculation thus made has been justified by the Charge actually in- 
curred within the period, Your Committee have called for an Account of the portion 
of the sum disbursed, under the general head of Charges Merchandize, which may 
justly be considered as chargeable to the Commercial branch of the Company's affairs 
athome. ‘The Total of these Charges on the goods in the Estimate is £. 5,135,409. 
The ‘Total of the adjusted Commercial Charges is £. 5,969,786 ; respecting which it is 
to be observed, that from the Company incurring many Charges of a Commercial 
nature exclusive of those dircctly on their Imports, it may be inferred that the pro- 
portion thus calculated upon those Imports is not far from a correct one.

The Trade from India is from its nature far more liable to be affected by contin- 
gencies than that from China, and especially from the circumstance of a very ma- 
terial part of the goods being purchased at the Sales in England for exporta- 
tion. The operations of the Act of 39th of Geo. III. already adverted to, for 
warehousing the goods, may be supposed to have produced some effect upon the 
Gross Produce of the Sales, which in the Estimate of 1793, and till the year 
1798-9, included the whole of the Customs payable upon the goods. The extent 
of the Sale Amount trom the years 1793-4 to 1796-7 considerably exceeded the 
Estimate; it fell below it in 1797-8, but in the next year it was more in a twofold 
degree, and from 1799-1800 to 1801-2 a considerable excess was maintained ; frem 
that period till the year 1808-9 a diminution is exhibited, but in 1809-10, the last 
ycar of the Account, a revival again appears. 


The extent of the Sale Produce of goods from India on the seventeen years, is 
on the average £. 2,637,746, exceeding the Estimate by £. 322,846. 


The Amount of the Sales of goods from China does not exhibit so much fluc- 
tuation as that from India. In three years, 1793-4, 1796-7, and 1797-8, it was 
below the Estimate ;. but in 1794-5 and 1795-6 it was above, and trom 1798-9 
to 1809-10 the excess was considerable in each year. On the average of the 
whole seventeen years, the Amount was £. 3,405,663, being more than estimated by 
47325263.

In the Estimate of 1793 the calculation of the Prime Cost of goods was made 
upon a rate of exchange different from that in the Estimate with which it is to be 
compared; and the Charges are proportioned at six instead of five er cent. upon 
the Sale amount, as in the latter Estimate; and considering that the comparison 
proposed could. not be correctly made without some alteration, Your Committee 
have caused an Estimate to be prepared, calculating the Prime Cost at the rates of 
exchange, and the Charges according to the principle required. 


The Result drawn by the Estimate in 1793 was on a calculation including the 
whole of the Customs, and on a Peace Freight ; whereas in the Estimate of the sub- 
sequent years, the whole of the Customs is only included for a part of the period, 
and the Freight is almost universally upon the principle of a War Freight, the difter- 
ence of which must have affected the Result in those years, but to what extent it is 
impossible to determine.

Your Committee feel it needless to explain particularly the fluctuations in the

Your Committce now proceed to consider the Amount received for Charges and 
Profit on Private Trade, which was £.2,440,937- 


This head of Receipt is not to Le assumed as entirely a Profit, because it is in part 
a reimbursement of the expense incurred upon the Goods of Privileged and Private 
‘Traders, from the time of landing them to their final delivery trom the Warehouses, 
cither to the original Owners or Consignees, or to the Purchasers. These trans- 
actions, in reference to the Privileged Traders, originated at the time of passing the Act 
of 1793, when eularged facilities were granted to individuals to participate in the 
commerce of the East, this Charge was then reduced from 7 per cent. to 3 per cent. to 
be levied as a Duty or allowance upon the Gross Sale Amount of all Imports by Private 


“ ‘Trade, over and above the Freight chargeable on the same. ‘The expenses of this 


description actually incurred by the Company upon these goods, being for the most 
part blended with their General Charges, it is not practicable to state with accuracy the 
net advantage accruing from this species of agency. It should however be remarked, 
in explanation of the excess which is apparent beyond what would arise on the Gross 
Sale Amount of Private Trade goods in the manner directed by the Act, that this 
head of Receipt includes likewise certain dues the Company receive upof: goods im- 
ported under an indulgence to the Commanders and Officers of their chartered Ships, 
which are calculated at various rates.

the Amount of £.2,992,440. 5s. reserving the sum of £.1,207,559. 15s. yielding an 
Interest of £. 36,226. 158. 10d. ‘The management of the Annuities, as to the payment of 
the Interest, was vested in the East India Company, and an allowance on that 
account was made by the Public up to the years 1793, when an Act was passed trans- 
ferring the whole to the Bank ; and the Principal Sum now rémaining due to the Com- 
pany on these Annuities, viz. £.1,207,559. 158. is the Amount payable by the Public on

The value of the Exports of Goods and Stores, shewn in the Appendix to the Third Appendix to 
Report, is calculated in the seasons September to September, whereas the Payments 5* Report, N° 5.

1 cause of it is to be found in the new arrangement of the Military system in 1796,

The Tea Duties, and the Amount of Bullion consigned to India for the purchase of 
Hemp on account of Government, not requiring observation, the only remaining 
head of the Expenditure on which explanation seems requisite, is the sum paid to 
the Captains of Ships worn out in the Service, amounting to £. 355,190. ‘This 
Payment is connected with the Charge for Freight. It is a temporary expense, as 
it began in 1796-7, and ended in the year 1803-4, and was occasioned by an altera- 
tion adopted by the Company in their Shipping system, about the year 1795. _-Ante- 
cedent to this period, a presumptive right to the commands of the Chartered Ships in 
the service, as to a species of Property, had been created by continued usage, so 
that when a Ship had run the number of voyages stipulated in the Charter-party, and 
became unfit for service, a claim was kept upon the part of the Owners to supply 
another Ship in her stead, and of the Captain to have the command of it when so sup- 
plied. ‘The abolition of this claim was necessary to the substitution of the new system, 
which rested upon the principle of open competition, and it was thought equitable on 
abolishing it, to make a proportioncd compensation to the Captains, which in the 
aggregate amounted to the sum above stated. A considerable saving of expense was 
anticipated from the measure. 


Although the question as to the degree in which this expectation was realized, does 
got fall within the immediate scope of the present discussion, Your Committee consider 
it an object of attention from its connection with the disbursements of the Company. 
Adverting to the rate of Freight now paid, on a comparison with the rate paid in the year 
1796, before the change of system, it is found that the present average rate on a Ship of 
800 tons for India, is £.42. 1s. 8d. perton, and that the rate paid in 1796 was £.42. 196.14. 
On a Ship of 1,200 tons for China, the present average rate is £.40. 5s. 4d. which 
in 1796 was £. 38. 5s. 10d. ; being less at the present period on a Ship of 800 tons, 
by 178. 5d. per ton, and more on a Ship of 1,200 tons, by £.1. 19s. 6d. per ton.

exclusive of the Insurance borne by the Company. iis, however, is not entirely a

That a very different Result from what has now been shown, might have been ex- 
spected, from the prospects held out in the year 1793, is not to-be denied. These 
prospects however were grounded on calculations to be realized only by the continuance 
sof peace. ‘The effect of a state directly the reverse, which has with little intermission - 
subsisted since that time, and which, in producing the most unfavorable influence a 
the Affairs of the Company abroad, could not fail to have one little less so.on those.al 
home, and, in fact, the pressure on the Treasury in England, with the interruption. of 
-resources, owing .both to European and Indian war, has been severely experienced ; 
though not perhaps to the degree naturally to have been apprehended, when the 
demands for India, great beyond the measure of all former precedent, are adverted 
to. Viewing the subject in this light, coupling it with the Charge arising out,of the 
Military arrangements in 1796, and the extraordinary increase in the Homé 
Expenditure, both Political and Commercial, incident to the war, that a Deficiency 
.should have occurred in the resources, and the necessity have arisen of resorting to 
-extraordinary assistance to meet circumstances of extraordinary difficulty, is not to 
-be wondered at. But it must not be forgotten, that this extraordinary aid has not 
been required by extraordinary demands for an Expenditure by which so much pro-

The Transactions which relate to Private and Neutral Trade, and to the sale of 
Prize Goods, are shewn separately at the bottom of the Statement. 


Although Your Committee have, in a former part of their Report, brought to the 
attention of the House the nature of the various Imports from the East under these 
heads, and the extent of them according to the Sale Amount, they conceive it pro- 
per here again to advert to the subject. In a former part of the Report it has been 
stated, that the Sale Producgof the Private ‘Trade Goods, from 1793-4 to 1809-10 
inclusive, amounted to the sam of £. 33,991,256. and of Neutral and Prize Goods 
to £. 3,803,601. together £ 37,794,857. 

Under their successive’ Charters of exclusive privilege, the Trade between Eng- 
land, and India and China, was in the strictest sense vested in the East India Com- 
pany, before the period of passing the Act in the year 1793; and till that time no 
British subject, either abroad or at home, could embark in it, except under the express 
|e prima of the Company, while the Commerce of Neutrals was wholly interdicted 

ill the passing of another Act in the year 1795. 

Any discussion of the particular causes which produced the Enactments, giving a 
limited admission to the Trade of individuals with India in the year 1793, is unne- 
cessary. 

To examine at large in what degree the intentions of the Legislature have been 
realized, is hardly consistent with the course which Your Committee have thought it 
their duty to adopt for the general conduct of their present enquiry, which has been 
studiously confined to the state of the Finances of the Company. Feeling, however, 
that a strict adherence to this line would admit of little tetoan. a mere Statement of 
the connection between the Sales of the Goods and the Receipts and Payments of 
the Home Treasury, they trust no improper deviation willl be imputed to them, if 
referring to the Documents already before the House, and others in the possession of

The species of Trade denominated in the Statement originally adverted to Neutral Appendix, N° 2& 
and Prize Goods, will not call for remark further thatras it passes through the medium of 
the Company. Its first appearance was in the year 1795-6, in consequence of the new 
state of affairs upon the Continent of Europe. About the latter end of the year 
1794, the French made their irruption into the United Provinces, which was followed by 
the conquest of the country. This event imposed on His Majesty's Governmentnew 
measures relative to the Dutch Trade with India and China, which was then con- 
siderable. These measures apply to this species of Trade, the provisions which 
governed the Indian Trade under the existing Laws. A special provision was at the 
same time made in favor of such Subjects of the United Provinces as maintained 
their allegiance to the Stadtholder and chose to avail themselves of it, by Orders of 
Council dated 16th and 21st January 1795, afterwards confirmed by the Act of the 
35th of the King, cap. 15. and again by another Act in the same year, cap. 80. and 
other Acts since passed.

Your Committee consider this Account as a general reply to the question proposed, 
and will only add such observations as are suggested by the examination of it. As 
the title-of this Account details all the Appropriations directed by the Act referred to, 
it only remains to enquire in what degree these Appropriations have been carried 
into effect. : 


‘The detail of this Account is principally extracted from that of the Statement of 
:the Cash Transactions, and’is drawn up exclusive of any Receipt-arising outdf the 
Credit of the Company. This mode of ‘Statement is conformable to the object in 
wiew, and to the literal directions of the Act. 


The Payment directed to precede all others, after the liquidation of ths Demands, 
-as described in the Act, Outgeings, and Expenses, is that of the Dividends; an 
Enactment, made no.doubt under the proviso that Funds should exist for the liquida- 
tion of the Demands first mentioned, antecedent to this Payment: although it is to be 
remarked that there is no restriction preventing the Company from paying the Divi- 
-dends from any other source whatever, in the event of the I'unds enumerated iv the 
Act proving in any:one ycar insuflicient for the discharge of the current Demands. 


Taking the aggregate Receipts and Payments of current Demands from 1793 to 
1810, there,will appear a Surplus in the Receipts, after the liquidation of all the 
Demands in question, in.some years, to. very considerable Amount; in others to an 
Amount exceeding that of the Dividends ; but in the years 1801-2, 1803-4, 1804-5, 
1806-7, and 1807-8, it was otherwise. It might be argued that the Payment of the 
Dividends in these years is not in literal conformity with the stipulations of the Act; 
Your Committee therefore think it their duty to observe, that a satisfactory justifica- 
tion of the Payment will be furnished by a consideration of the circumstances in which 
the Company stood at the period at which it occurred. That the actual Cash Funds 
-of the Company were then below the Amount required cannot be disputed, but the 
cause of it must in justice be adverted to; Monies had been advanced by the Com- 
pany in India and Europe, om account of the ‘Public, to a very considerable Amount. 
Had their Demand upon this account, which, according to their own shewin, 
amounted in 1801 to £. 2,672,400, and in 1803 to £.3,573;339, been Tiquidated, 
their Treasury would have been amply replenished, and the Deficiency in those 
years prevented.. Even in 1803-4 the. re-payment made was only in the sum of 
_£-1,000,000, and in the following they received nothing, notwithstanding the Debt - 
-of the Public to the Company had increased to £.4,018,000. In the year 1805-6, ” Tid. 
-oua Report of Your Committee, a Million was voted to the Company in part Fiqui- 
-dation of tueir claim, and the Surplus Receipt exceeded the sum required for pay- 
ament of the Dividend ; but in the next year, notwithstanding a further vote of a 
Million, 2 Deficiency again appears, and in the year 1807-8 the Surplus ‘of the Pay- 
"ments beyond the Receipts was very considerable. ‘At this’ period the claim of the’ - 
“Company is stated at £.2,460,000. In the year 1808-9 Your Committee having Ibid, 
made a final examination of these Claims, the sum of £.1,500,000-was voted by the 
House, and a Surplus Receipt was accordingly produced in a largé Amount in that 
and the following years. From the above explanations it: is clear that every sup- 
posed departure from the direct letter of the Act, in these instances, is tobe imputed 
to the disappointments experienced by the Company in the recovery of their Claims 
on advances for the Public Service. ‘The remarks already made relate principally

‘The last column of this Account is termed Government for Participation, and 
velates to the payment to be made by the Company into His Majesty's Exchequer, 
sagreeably to the stipulation of the Act of the 33d. cap, 52. sect. 111. the more parti- 
-cular consideration of which was deferred in a former part of this Report. 


This stipulation was founded on an agreement between His Majesty's Govern- 
ment and the East India Company, that the Public were eventually entitled toa 
-certuin portion ef the Profits accruing to the Company from the. prosperity of their 
Revenve and Commerce. According to the mode of calculation laid down in the 
Act, this conditional Participation could accrue only from the following seurces, viz. 
:from the Surplus remaining of the net Proceeds of the Sales of Goods at home, from 
:the Duties and Allowances arising by Private Trade, and from all ether Profits of the 
Company in Great Britain, after providing for the payment of Bills of. Exchange 
already accepted; for the current Payment of ether Debts, Interest, and other 
Outgoings, Charges and Expenses; (the Bead Debt computed in another part of the 

-clause at £. 1,500,000 always excepted) for a Dividend on the Capital Stock at 10 per 
-cent. per annum, ‘increased to 103; and lastly, for Bills of Exchange in liquidation of 
sthe Debt contracted in India, to the extent of £. 500,000 per annum. Provision 
having been made for these several Payments, the annual sum payable to the 
Public in the way of Participation, was fixed at £. 500,000, to be set apart hali- 
yearly, on the 1st July and the 1st January in cach year, beginning with July 1793. 
Provisions were likewise made in the Act to ensure punctuality in the payment of 
sthese sums into His Majesty's Exchequer ; but it was enacted, that in the event of a 
Deticiency in the Amount of- the Proceeds (after making the Payments to which 
-precedence was given) arising from extraordinary Expenses incurred in time of war, 
-or preparations for war, or from cireumstances incidental to war, that the 
Deficiency or Deficiencies were net to be made good from the Surplus of the 
‘future year or years, but were to be dtectned a Debt to be made good to the Public 
sat the determination of the exclusive ‘Trade of the Company, in case their ene 
Assets:

The Payments shewn in the years 1793-4 and 1794-5, from having been made 
when a Deficiency of-Funds for the purpose, according to the privciple of Participa- 
tion laid down, is fully apparent, Your Committee think it right to state to the 
House, that a reference to the 124th section will furnish an explanation of the trans- 
action, by shewing that the Payment was specifically directed to take place antecc- 
dent to the addition of the £ per cent. to the Dividends of the Capital Stock, and that 
it must be considered to have been made from the Balance of Cash in the hands of the 
Company, distinct from their net Proceeds of the year. 


As to the Sources from which the Participation of the Public was to be derived, 
namely the Surplus Proceeds, &c. as described in the beginning of the section, Your 
Committee cannot avoid reverting to the Estimates on which this arrangement was 
evidently founded, and again remarking that the Supply of a Million annually from 
the Surplus Revenue in India, as directed in the 107th section, must have been 
assumed as the basis of the expectations then held out to the Public, because it seems 
clear that the Surplus Proceeds in contemplation by the 111th section of the Enact- 
ment, were in reality the combined Profit derived from Revenue and Commerce. 
And this conclusion is further supported by provision being nade for failure of payment 
in the event of a Deficiency of Surplus Proceeds happening from war. As the Deft- 
ciency which has in fact existed from the time of passing the Act, is to be ascribed to 
the wars in Thdia and Europe, no further Payment has been made to the Public under 
the directions of the Act, but Your Committee observing that in some years a Surplus 
of Funds is shewn in the Account notwithstanding the war ye making the payments 
for Dividends, and on Bills of Exchange for Indian Debt) have thought it necessary 
to ascertain and to state to the House the causes why payment was not made on the 
Participation in such years. 


The Payments stipulated by the Act considerably excecded the Funds in the first 
year from which such Payments were to be made, consequently recourse was had to 
Funds that could on no consideration be looked upon as Profit, the only source from 
which the Proceeds described could be derived. ‘The excess of Payment thus made 
was supplied by Monies raised by the Company, either on new Capital or on Bond, in 
excess of the £.1,500,000, to which that Debt was then limited, and became a Debt 
ayable from the net Proceeds, taking priority of the public claim to Participation. 
The Deficiency ef Funds for the liquidation of this claim is shewn by an Account 
inserted in the Appendix. Appendix, Ne 4p. 


From a variety of circumstances therefore, but chiefly from those consequent upon 
war, the net Proceeds of the Company's Treasury in Great Britain have not been 
sufficient for the payment of the Participation to the Public according to the Act, and 
with the exception of the sum of £. 500,000 paid in the manner above described, the 
whole has fallen in arrear, and become a Debt due by the Company under the 122d 
section, subject however to the reservation contained in the Act as to the liquidation 
of it, that is “ in the event only of the Company's General Assets amounting in 
“ value to more than sufficient for the payment of all their just Debts and the reali- 
“ zation of their Capital Stock.” .

The value of the Assets on the 1st March 1810 is stated at £. 14,504,944. 
Deduceting from it their Amount on. the 1st March 1793, there will be an Increase in 
the sum of £.4,764,112. The Increase thus shewn, however, calls for some 
observation and adjustment. 


The value of ‘Assets under the head of Goods in. the Warehouse unsold in each 
of the periods, is computed on Estimate governed by the sale price at the time, and 
conscquently includes the Profit after defraying all Charges. As the value of goods at 
the latter period very considerably exceeded at the former, the computed Profit 
on the 1st March 1810 was likewise much greater. The excess amounted to 

Appendix, X° 50. _£. 998,000, and should be deducted from the Increase of the Assets, because, although 
it may fairly be assumed as a future available Profit, it has no immediate reference to 
the Cash proceedings of the period. Credit is likewise taken for the sum of 

Appendix, N°23. £. 960,000 as a claim upon Government for Stores supplied, Advances, &c. This. 
article cannot but be considered as disputable, if not wholly objectionable, if reference 
is had to the Balance settled and paid after the Report of Your Committee in 1808, 
although it may not from its connection with the Disbursements, be excluded in the 
view to be now given. Deducting therefore the increased Amount of the Profits, viz. 
£- 998,000, from the additional Amount of the Assets as above shewn, the Increase in 
the period will be reduced to £.3,766,112. The Increase of the Debts has been 
shewn to amount to £. 2,366,010, consequently an improvement would at first view 
be apparent in the sum of £.1,400,102. The Money raised in the year 1793 upon

the whole Concern upon the Balance of Property generally.

Tu endeavoring to account for the alteration of the Balance which has thus been 
ascertained, Your Committee cannot avoid stating that they do not undertake the task 
with the same degree of confidence as they would have done could their conclusions 
have been supported throughout by actual Accounts. In a material branch of this 
enquiry they have been obliged to content themselves with Estimates, the necessity 
of which they trust they have satisfactorily shewn in a former part of the Report. 
‘The same necessity now exists in an equal degree, as the Result of the Commercial 
Affairs can only be drawn upon that principle. - 


‘The connection between the Political and the Commercial branches of the Concern, 
being so strict as to render.it wholly impracticable to make a proper distinction, 
Your Committée have divided the subject into three heads, viz. Territorial or Political; 
doubtful as to the part Territorial or Commercial ; and Commercial; and from the 
consideration that it would be the most intelligible manner of bringing it into view, a 
Statement has been drawn up and added to the Appendix, shewing the various 
Charges classed under the above heads respectively. As the detail of the items so 
classed have becn selected from the mass of the Accounts in the Appendixes of this 
and former Reports, and have.for the most part already been the subject of remark, 
the only observations now requisite are those which relate to the combination 
proposed. 


The extent in which the Political branch of the Affairs has contributed to produce 
the Balance, is stated at the sum of £. 6,364,931; which sum results from adding to 
the Surplus Charge of India every other positive expense belonging to the Territories 
which had not -been included in tHe Accounts of Revenues and Charges annually 
presented to the House, being in the greatest part Disbursements made in England, 
cither by His Majesty's Paymasters General for the troops serving in India, or by the 
Company at home for Freight of Military, or the expense considered to have becn 
incurred under this head, ~ ~ 


The Charge of the Settlements of Prince of Wales Island, Bencoolen, and 
St. Helena in a small degree, has been blended in the Territorial Accounts with the 
other Charges, and was defrayed mostly by Supplies from Bengal. ‘Ihe Amount so 
cartied to Account was £.2,817,146. It being very questionable whether these 
Settlements are more requisite for Political or Commercial objects, the above sum has 
becn deducted from this head and added to the second. The excess of Political 
Charge or Expense is exhibited at £.14,936,230. A considerable part of this sum 
consisted of Supplies and Advances for the Public Service, and in the expense of 
Expeditions, for which, upon an agreement with His Majesty's Government, the 
Company were to be reimbursed. The adjusted Amount of repayments in Cash, in 
Advances by the Paymasters General, &c. is stated at £. 8,571,299, and the net 
Excess of Political Charge is then £.6,364,931, as before shewn. 


The Total of the part termed Doubtful as to its application, is £.5;953,660. On 
this head it is only necessary to remark, that an adjustment has been made in the

The Result of the whole Financial Transactions of the East India Company during 
the period to which the examination of Your Committee has extended, namely from 
1792-3 to 1808-9 abroad, and from 1793-4 to 1809-10 at home, has been stated 
to exhibit a Deficiency of £. 11,020,556 on the comparison of the Balances at the 
commencement and at the close of it. The causes of this Deficiency have been ex- 
plained to be mostly in the excess of Disbursement beyond the Revenue‘in the ‘Ter- 
ritorial part of the Coucern, which is to be traced to the circumstances of the time 
having been such as to lead to unprecedented Expenditure both from the Indian and 
Home Treasuries. ‘To what extent the Disbursements of the former were affected, 
the Charges sufficiently shew, while the degree in which those of the latter have been 
enhanced, it is extremely difficult to calculate with accuracy, although the Profit 
upon the Trade has been stated to exceed by £. 2,164,533, the Amount required to’ 
defray the Expenses and Losses immediately incident to it, and to pay the Divi- 
sdends on the Capital Stock, with the Interest on the-Bonds, 


Your Committee having referred in their Third Report to considerations that 
scemed, in their judgment, to offer some counter-balance to the sacrifices of Funds 
which had been made, conceive it unnecessary to introduce any additional remarks on 
this head; but aiter calling to the recollection of the House, that the observations 
hitherto made on these extensive and complicated Transactions, and on the Result 
of them, have applied exclusively to the interests of the East India Company, Your 
Committee will procced to submit their view of them in their bearing on the general 
interests of the British Empire, which they trust is such as to lead to Results much 
more gratifying than those which have been exhibited in reference to the separate 
Affairs of the Company. The Invoice value of Goods and Stores exported by the

Appendix, No, 41. 
EXTRACT of Minutes of Court of DireGors, dated 20th January 1705. 


‘THE Solicitor reported to the Court, that the Appeal in the Chinfurah Cause was heard on 
‘Saturday laft, before the Lords of Council for Prize Caufes; when, after full argument, their 
Lordfhips were pleafed to affirm the order-of the Judge of the: Admirelty, as to his opinion that 
the Goods contratted for at the time of the capture of Chinfurah, for the Dutch Inveftment to 
Europe, remaining in the hands of the Manufacturers or at the Fadories diftant from Chinfurah, 
were to be confidered as a part of the Goods feized and taken at the furrender of the Town and 
Fort of Chinfurah, and to be-accounted for to the Captors of Chinfurah; ‘but that the Company is 
entitled to be allowed all their Advances and Charges on fuch Goods;—and referred the caule 
‘back to the Court below to fettle the Account,

Can you detail those inconveniences ?—One of the principal inconveniences is, that the 
periods at which we ere forced to apply for the tonnage, are such as will not admit our 
calculating with any degree of nicety what tonnage we shall require in the course of that 
season; the month of September was that in which our applications for tonnage were de- 
manded from us inIndia, and at that period of the year the principal article of exportation, I 
allude to Indigo, from our port of Calcutta was not then manufactured in such a degree as 
to enable us to say how much we should require tonnage for ; the price of the freight demanded 
by the Hondarable Company completely prevents us from shipping many gruff goods, and 
even comes too heavy upon such as Indigo and other goods of greater value; we have been 
charged as high in the year 1806 as £. zi 
ship on regular Ships, because theré“Were no extra Ships, none of that'sort of ‘tonnage 
which the Ret of Parliament intended us to be supplied with, in India. 

The inconvenience arising from the being obliged to ask the quantity of tonnage before. 
you can ascertain your quantity of , Must it not be attended with either making you

“ir you happen to demand too much, does the Company make you bay the freight upon

"Supposing you demanded too little, could you at all times with facility procure the

Board of Trade at Calcatta would have allowed individual to fillit; but I have known

Have the extra Ships with the private trade sailed at fixed periods ?~On the contrary ;

For which of course he charges you Interest and Commission ?—Always.

“Ww hen your goods arrive here, or when you export from this country to India, are there
