venience, irom being disappointed of the freight for which Ehad applied, “I will if you 
please state a specific case, a recent one; in April 1805 I applied for tonnage in order to 
export goods that were commissioned from a House of business in Calcutta: these 
were directed about three months afterwards to be shippéd-on the Northumberland ; part of 
these goods were left out for want of tonnage. Those were the last ships'sailing ; it being in 
the month of June, the ships Northumberland and Euphrates had both a circuitous Voyage 
to muke ; that is to say, they were to go toSt. Helena before proceeding to India, which was a 
disadvantage. Some of the goods I have mentioned were left out, for want of tonnage, although: 
the freight fur the whole had been paid in to the Company's proper Offices: these goods, so left 
out, I naturally expected would be shipped by the first ships of the following season ; they 
were not, nor upon the second Fleet of that next season ; they were shipped in May 1806, 
being above twelve months after the application for freight was made, in the Tottenham. In 
consequence of this delay of twelve months in the shipment, the House who commissioned 
those goods from India refused to receive them, and they were sold for our account, who 
were the Shippers, to a very considerable loss; conceiving myself entitled to look to the 
Honse who ordered these goods, for a loss that derived itself from no fault of mine, but 
solely from the tonnage not being allotted upon earlier ships, I am at this moment engaged 
in a controversy with the House who ordered the goods, in order to recover this loss, which 
he disputes, upon the ground that he did not receive his goods in due time. Another incon- 
yenience which I have experienced is, that when the application is made for freight to the 
_ Honourable the Court of Directors, not knowing when it will be granted, I dare not orderto 
be packed a variety of. ls that are of a perishable nature, until I am told shat tonnage 
is ready to receive it, This is frequently done at a fortnight’s notice ; that is to say, I am told 
that op such a day in about a fortnight you must have the goods ready for shipping: during 
that pruot it is impossible to purchase, pack, and prepare for shipping, goods, some of 
which may come from distant manufacturing towns, and some by water, of which the’ 
passage is uncertain; provided the goods are not ready upon the day that is notified, there 
js a fine chargeable upon every package, which 1 myself have never paid, but I have known 
it to be paid by others. :

SirJOHN ANSTRUTHER, Baronet, in the Chair. 
Mr. Henry Trail, called in, and examined. 


IT has been stated to us, that there is a considerable difficulty arises to the Private Mer- 
chants from their being obliged to insure on ship or ships, instead of being able to insure upon 
individual ships, from the mode in which the trade is now carried on; is that so?—It is. 

Is there any considerable difference between the rates of Insurance upon ship or ships, 
and upon an individual ship ?—Yes, generally a difference of two or three per cent. 

Can you with the same facility obtain an Insurance upon ship or ships to a large extent, 
as you could upon individual sheer no means. 

hat isthe reason of that ?—The dislike the Underwriters have to insure generally arises 
from the fear of having their interest all upon one bottom, instead of being divided into 
several risks. 

Has it ever happened to you to meet with that difficulty ?—It has. 

Have you any objection to state the case ?—There has not been any recent instance ; but 
three or four years ago we had a very large sum to get covered upon ship or ships, which we 
effected with a good deal of difficulty. 

Did youeffect it all at once?—The first sum we effected in the course of a few days; a 
fresh order-came for a larger sum to be covered in the same manner : we were advised by 
our broker at Lloyd’s to postpone effecting the second insurance until we could advise the 
Underwriters of the ships’ names upon which the goods composing the first insurance were 
shipped, from the fear of having their former risks increased.” 

id you follow that advice ?—We did. “ 

How long was it between the period of the one and the other ?—About three months. 

Then during that three months was the second sum uncovered ?—It was waiting for the 
advice of the ships’ names on which the goods were laden. 

You effected the Insurance upon the second sum three months after ?—Not so soon; ac- 
counts arrived of the capture of the Althea, which occasioned an immediate rise in the pre- 
mium of from 15 to 25 percent. 

Did you effect the insurance at 25 per cent. ?—We were obliged todo it; we waited two 
months, in hopes that the premium would fall to its former rate, but it did not, and we ef- 
fected the Insurance at 25 Guineas. 

The former Insurance I think you said was effected at 15?—It was. The same ship 
that brought the account of the capture of the Althea, brought the account of the ship- 
ment of the goods contained in the first Policy, or about the same time. 

At the time you first received the order for the second Insurance, if you had been able to 
have specified the names of the particular ships upon which the goods were to be laden, 
could you have effected the Insurance at Lloyd’s?—I have no doubt of it, 

With regard to the times at which goods are shipped in Bengal, I believe the Merchants 
in Bengal are under the necessity of informing the Board of Trade at a given period of the 
year, in August or September, I think ?—We are called upon to specify the quantity of 
tonnage we shall want in the ensuing shipping season. 

Does any inconvenience result from that ?—It sometimes happens that the Merchant has 
not the means of ascertaining what quantity of goods he will have to ship, and therefore he 
sends in his application at a Fazard of having too much or too little. 

Did it ever happen to 0 your House to pay any forfeit for having asked for more tonnage 
than you found you should have occasion for ?—On one occasion it has. 

Did you pay forfeit ?@—Yes, 

‘What was the amount of it?—About 5,000 Rupees. 

Are there any inconveniences experienced by* the Merchants from the circumstance of 
the uncertainty of the time of sailing of the ships, or the uncertainty of loading their 

?—There is an inconvenience in not being able to give orders about our Insurances ; 
we must do it generally, instead of upon ‘Poroeular ships. 

I believe you are not a Ship-owner?—I am not 3 

Are you of opinion that if the Merchants were allowed to load their own ships at their 
own times, and in their own way, that the trade between Europe and India, and India and 
Europe, would be considerably increased or not ?—I am strongly of opinion that it would 
considerably increase. 

In both ways?—Not so mych out as from India. 

Are you or not of opinion that in time of peace you could meet the Americans and other 
foreigners in the market of Europe, if the restrictions that are now imposed upon the 
private trade were removed ?—I should suppose nearly so. 

In time of war, supposing a double duty laid upon foreigners in India, and the Americans 
obliged to make a circuitous Voyage by Ameriea, do you think if the restrictions were 
removed, that you could meet the Americans in time of war ?—It would be more y 
- equality; I think we could supply the Europe market as cheap as they could in time 
of war. 

I believe your House in India never were Ship-owners ?—They never were. 

I believe your's was one of the largest Agency-houses in Calcutta ?—It was reckoned so. 

‘Will you'explain more in detail how the increase in the exports to and from India pe 


on the Affairs of The EAST INDIA COMPANY. | 93 


take place upon the change of system ?—I think it would only apply to the raw materials, 
and not to the manufactured goods from India. 

With regard to the exports from this Country, how do you conceive they would be 
enlorged ?—1 am not aware that they would be materially affected by the indulgence pre- 
sumed, only that they would go out at a lower rate of freight, and be therefore supplied 
cheaper than they now are. I do not suppose the consumption could be increased. 

Upon the supposition of the proposed enlargement, would it be practicable always to 
insure from India upon specific ships ?~That would depend upon having opportunities to 
me home for insurance, and upon a certainty of getting those goods shipped upon par- 
ticular vessels.

“Sir JOHN ANSTRUTHER, Baronet, in the Chair. 
Mr. John Bebb, again called in, and examined. 


Mr. Bebb. I beg leave to offer some explanations of some of the evidence I gave on 
“Thursday last. I stated that when the Company’s Ships were taken up, they were taken up. 
at £.16 per ton for heavy goods, and £.20 a ton for piece goods ; that freight was paid in 
Bengal three fourths in advance, and of course it assisted the owners with capital, and 
saved them interest and risk. I think I stated that.from the skill of their servants and their 
capital, the Company could carry on trade with more advantage than individuals. I would add, 
that the Company’s goods have a character for exccllence, which the goods of private per- 
‘sons do not attain; this gives the Company a considerable advantage in the Europe market, 
A foreign Merchant can give bis correspondent in London an order to purchase Company's 
goods, with confidence that the goods wiil prove of the quality he desires; in respect of the 
goods of individuals, he is at an uncertainty; he must trust to the judgment and attention 
of his correspondent, and is liable to disappointment in the quality of the goods. The 
Company's goods sell at a higher price than the goods of private persons, even though 
such goods may happen to be equal in quality to the Company's. When engaged on my 
own account in correspondence to this countty from Bengal, I conceived the difference to 
be equal to fifteen per cent. on piece goods, though my goods were provided by myself with 
great care and attention. The commission which falls upon the goods of Private Merchants 
at the different places of purchase, shipment and sale, except where the owner himself may 
reside, in their transit from the place of produce in Bengal, through Calcutta and London, 
to the place of consumption abroad, by its repetition acts with a pressing weight upon the 
produce of goods, and abates the profit, or eventually creates a loss or tends to it; some of 
the rates of commission were 10 per cent. for procuring gaods at the place of manufacture, 
te and a half per cent. for shipping, and two and a half per cent. on gross sales in 
ndon. $ 

1 wish to add to my answer to another point where a foreign State in Europe ‘may 
determine to support its own.commerce by high duties, or where prohibited altogether the 
introduction of fodian articles, except in its own ships, it will supply itself with Indian 
goods directly from India as far as its credit or the proceeds of its native productions or its

will it share in the commerce to and from India, and so, fr counteract. the notion of

How far do you think aay regulation on our‘part might be made to operate against the 
foreign trade as you describe ?—I apprehend it will be checked in some degree by higher 
dutics and higher port charges ; but the former must be laid ow with judgment, or else the 
goods will be smuggled om board of foreign ships, and evade the duties altogether. 

Would not it follow from that mode of reasoning, that the Company, in a commercial 
point of view, have nothing whatever to fear from the trade being thrown open to the com- 
petition of Private Merchants, whether in India or in Europe ?—I have often reflected uj 
the subject, and I have been of the same opinion for twenty years, that they would have 
nothing to fear in a point of view merely commercial, : 

Then supposing the Company’s exclusive privilege to cease, and that they were in future 
to carry on their trade as a Chartered Company, which they would remain in common with 
the other Merchants of this country or India, do you think that the Company could carry. 
on their trade under these circumstances to greater advantage than tite Private Merchants?— 
Certainly ; but in such case it could not be expected that they should export articles of 
national manufacture to a loss as they now do, or import from India articles for the benefit 
of Government on the terms they often now import them. 

What articles do the Company import into this country for the use of Government ex- 
cept Saltpctre ?—At present they bring Sunn-hemp for the service of Government, without 
any profit whatever. é 

his is the first year I believe that they have brought any ?— Yes, on Government account; 
but they are under a disadvantage in bringing it in proportion as they may lose by the dead 
weight necessary to be put on the ship ; and some years ago, on the occasion of the first 
rupture with Russia, they brought it on their own account, at the wishes or at the instances 
of His Majesty’s ministers, for the purpose of answering the national exigencies, and they. 
Jost greatly by it. 

Did they bring a large quantity ?—A considerable quantity. 

Do you apprehend that under the present circumstances of the East India ‘Company, they 
navigate their regular ships as cheaply as the Private Merchants could navigate their own 
ships ?—Not having experience in shipping on my own account, I cannot answer the question 
decidedly ; but the ships are taken up by open competition, and they have an advantage 
in being at a considerable less insurance than the private ships. 

When you state the commission that is paid upon providing private goods in India, do 
you on the other hand state the charges of all the Commercial Extablishinenes that the Com- 
pany have been at in India ?—The regular Establishment is not added to the invoice. 

Is there any warehouse rent added to the invoice ?—No, 

Have the expenses of the building and purchasing the warehouses in India been added

Is it not optional for every Owner to tender at such rate of freight as he thinks fit ?—Cer~

have been stored exactly and fitted as they were, nor diverted to political purposes, except in 
extreme necessity, which was the occasion of the low rate of freight at which I tendered, and

Whether in the terms and conditions published by the Court of Directors as the ground 
on which tenders were to be made, the manner of storing those Ships was not expressly de- 
elared?—I think in that instance that though the terms’ and conditions where the schedule

ceived from my general conversation with some of the Directors and parts of the Committee

extreme necessity.

be employed on political services ?—Certainly.

been arranged, I could not have been disappointed. 3 : 

But generall speaking, is not the manner of fitting out the ships of the Company known

mands.

Sir William Bensley’s first Voyage 


This ship was originally ordered afloat in 
May 1802, bound to Bengal direct, and to 
be in the Downs 2d June 1802. 


I requested to be permitted to bring the 
ship afloat with some ships that were to be 
in the Downs fourteen days before that 
time, which was granted, on my agreeing to 
stay 14 days longer than usual in India be- 
tore I claimed demurrage. 


The cause for this request was, to save 
the south-west monsoon up the Bay of Bengal. 


A few days before my time for sailing from 
Gravesend, I was ordered to the Cape, and 
on the 18th May (in writing) to prepare 
water and provisions, &e. for the conveying 
90 troops irom the Cape to India. 


The water, &c. was sent from London, 
and the ship sailed on the 26th for the 
Downs, with a foul wind at N. E. (although 
fair from thence for India,) and actually 
passed through on the goth May at the tail 
ofa N. E, wind, which had been blowing 
rom the 2oth May, thé time I should have 
been there, if not detained for political neni 
: yn 


The expense I incurred by getting the shi 
ready, wll shew my idea of the value or 
time at that period, but which the subsequent 
act of the Court rendered nugatory ; on set- 
tling the freight account of that voyage, three 
days demurrage was deducted from my ac- 
counts, in consequence of this agreement, the 
ship having through the Downs three 
days before the 2d June. 


The Committee will here perceive, by my 
exertions in getting the water, X&c. &c. on 
board, the continued idea of the value of 
time at that period.

As it appears that by insuring on ship or ships generally, the premium is much higher 
han by insuring on specific supe, and the return, in case of loss, proportionably less, what 
is the method the Merchants take to cover themselves from this excess of Joss in such cases? 
—If I have £.100 to insure from India, and the premium is fi percent. I value my 
goods in the Policy at £.100. In that case, if the ship is totally lost or captured, I recover 
net £.03.- If I am obliged to give fifteen guineas per cent. I must value my goods higher, 
in order to save myself in case of Joss, a3 I have no return of the fifteen guineas; ‘t therefore 
value my goods, say at £.125 and then in case of loss I recover net £.105. 68, 3d. The 
result of this is, that in case of loss I save myself; but if the goods arrive, | have paid more 
premium than otherwise I should have done upon a single ship.

No. 1. 


East India House, 12th November 1806. 
Terns and Coxprtioys under which the East India Company are willing to furnish Tonnage, 
exclusive of that to be provided by the Act of the ggd of His present Majesty, cap. 52. 
1.—TIAT the applications for tonnage be received on the first Wednesday in the months of 
September, December, and March in each year, and that such applications be indorsed, 
“ Private Application for ‘Tonnage ;” and that any application made in the intermediate months, 
unléss Fequired by advertisement, will be considered only in the ensuing quarter. 


2.—That all applications be made by the persons who actually ship the goods, and not by any 
agent or clerk, and specify that the said goods are bona fide intended to be sent to India on 
account of the persons making the application, or on commission received from persons in India, 
whose names must be inserted in the applications; and the person making application must 
engage to verify the same by affidavit, if so required by the Couft of Directors. 


3.—That every application do specify the tonnage of measurable and heavy goods respectively, 
the particular articles of which each species of tonnage con the Presidencies to which they 
are to be consigned, and the periods when the same will be ready to be shipped. , 

4-—Thag no material deviation be permitted in the articles of tonnage specified in any request, 
after such request shall have been granted. ' 

5<—That no application for a less quantity than’ one ton be granted, 

6.—That the Court of Directors, in order to encourage the export of a sufficient supply of 
necessary articles for consumption in India, do not intend to restrain the exportation wholly to the 
letter of the Act, which limits the articles to such as are of the growth, produce, or manufacture 
of Great Britain, but the Court reserve to themselves the power of limiting the exportation of 
articles which are not of the growth, produce, or manofacture of Great Britain, or the exportation 
of which by individuals is not permitted by the Act, to such quantities as the Court may judge 
proper, And they farther reserve to themselves a power to reduce the quantities of any particular 
description of goods applied for by any individual, which may appear to them to operate to the 
exclusion of others. ¢ 

7.—That not more than fifty chests of wine, or fifty hogsheads of beer belonging to one person, 
be laden on any ship. 

8.—That the tonnage of wines or chests of liquors on freight, be calculated at two chests, 
containing twelve dozen quart bottles each to the ton, and not at three chests to the tou, ws has! 
occasionally been the practice heretofore, 


” : { 
9:—That the Tonnage of Carriages on freight be caleulated as follows, vis.

10.—That not more than two four-wheel carriages, or four two-wheel carriages, be laden on 
any ship, nor any oné house be permitted to ship more than one carriage on each ship. 

11.—That if quicksilver be allowed to he shipped oa freight, no expense or risk thereby 
be incurred by the Company or owners of the ship. 

12,—That the peace rate of freight for goods shipped in England on extra ships for India, 
be at a rate not exceeding £.5. per ton; and that such additional freight be paid for goods 
shipped in England in war, as the circumstances of the time may render necessary. 

13.—That the peace rate of freight homeward shall not exceed {.11. per ton; and that 
such additional freight be paid on goods laden in India on extra ships, in war, as the circun- 
stances of the time may render necessary. 

14.—That wine freighted from Madeira to India, on the Company’s extra ships, be at the rate 
of £.5. per pipe of 110 gallons. i 

15.—That the same rate of (reight be paid for wine sent from Madeira to any partof India, both 
in peace and war.

16.—That the freight of wine brought from India to England be £.8 per pipe in time of 
peace, and £.12 per pipe in time of war, and that this freight be paid previous to the delivery 
of the wine in England, and charged at the above. rates respectively, whether the pipes contain 


the full quantity or not. ‘ & 

17.—That persons requiring tonnage for wine from Madeira to be landed in India, or to be 
carried to India and from thence to England, be permitted to lade in articles for Madeira, freight 
free, to the amount of the tonnage they may be dllowed in wine, and that two pipes be cal- 


culated equal to one ton. 

18.—That the ships be allowed to remain at Madeira two working days for every twenty 
tons of goods they may have been permitted cither to carry to or receive on board at that 
island (the days of arrival and sailing not included), and thatif the agents of the shippers shouli 
not complete their lading within that period, the ships do preceed on their voyage, and the 
freight paid in England do thereby become forfeited. 

19.—That all persons do make a deposit in the Company’s treasury, within fifteen days after 
their requests to ship goods or wine shall have been granted by the Court of Directors, of the 
amount of freight chargeable on such goods or wine at the rates above mentioned, under the 
regulations of the Act. 

20.—That the Court of Directors do reserve to themselves the right of allotting to any of the 
sbips in their service, bound to the respective places of consignment, the goods or wine in such 
proportions as they may think proper; at the same time, the Court will endeavour to comply, as 
far as circumstances will admit, with the particular wishes of the proprietors, respecting the ship- 
ping of their goods or wine. 

* 

21,—That if the goods allotted as, above-mentioned be not sent on board the ships, previous’ to 
the day appointed by the Court for the ships clearing out at the Custom House, the freight paid on 
such goods shall be forfeited. 

22:—That should the produce of such goods or wine be paid into the Company's Treasury at 
either of the three Presidencies, or Bencoolen, bills will be granted on the Court of Directors, on 
the terms of the season allowed to other individuals, _ 

29-—That the proprietors of goods shall be exactly on a similar footing with the Company, in 
respect to short delivery, as is contained in the terms and conditions under which the ships shall 
have been engaged, 

24.—That each shipper of goods, jointly with the Company, shall be entitled to all allowance for 
ship damages and short delivery, not exeeeding £.4. per ton on their respective tounage; that is 
to say, £.4. per ton to such persons who occupy the like proportion of tonnage out and home, 
whether the damage be on the outward or homeward goods, and £.2. per ton on the outward 
goods, and the like sum on the homeward goods, when they belong to different proprictors, 
averaging on the whole at the rate of £.5. per ton on the builder’s measurement, agreeably to the 
terms under which the ships sball have been engaged. _ ‘ 

25.—That in all other cases the owners of goods will be subject to the same decisions and 
determinations only, as the Company themselyes are liable to. 

26.—That the tonnage of all goods (except the articles before mentioned) be calculated accord- 

_ ing to the computation of tonnage used by the Company. 

27.—That three days at least shall be appointed by the Court for shipping goods on board of each 
ship appointed to carry out the same, and that public notice shall be given, at least three days 
before such day of shipping, by the officer for private trade outwards. 

28.—That not any order will be given by the officer in the private trade department outwards, 
for goods allowed to be shipped on freight, until the several petsons who are permitted to export 
‘the same shall have delivered into the office an exact account of the tonnage of each article which 
they have been allowed to ship. 

29.—That before any goods shall be shipped, the same shall be registered with the officer for 
private trade outwards, in books to be kept by him for that purpose, which registry shall describe 
the marks and numbers of each bale or package of goods to be shipped, and the amount of the whole 
tonnage allowed to the person so shipping, and all guods which shall be shipped without being so 
registered, will be considered as goods illicitly shipped, and the goods will be subject to such seizure 
and forfeitures, and the owners, shippers, and agents concerned therein, to such forfeitures and 
Penalties, as any person shall be subject to by law, for carrying on trade toand from the East Indies 
without the Company’s licence. 

30.—Thit the said officer for private trade outwards, upon such registry as aforesaid, shall give an 
order or licence, under his hand, for the shipping of such goods, whieh licence, together with the 
goods, shall be carried to the East India Wharf to the proper officers there, whe shall examine the 


same, to see that the packages containonly the sorts of goods of which notice shall have been given,

tity of goods shipped, exceeding the quantily appertaining to-such sbipper as aforesaid, if the same 
shall amount to one ton or upwards, or single freight if under one ton. 

31.—That after the goods shall have been examined as aforesaid, the same shall be sent from the

hoyage being previously paid by the owner of the said goods, in deftult of which payment, the 
goods may be stopped. 

32.—Thaton the goods being shipped, bills of lading shall be signed for the same, in triplicate, 
by the commander or purser, which shall be delivered to the shipper of the goods, or his agent, 
the persons who sign such bills of lading being allowed, if they think proper, to add the following 
memorandum, in regard to the delivery of the goods at their consigned port, viz. “‘ To bedeli- 
« vered at the consigned port, provided the destination of the ship shall not be changed by the 
« East India Company, or their agents abroad, or by the act of any of His Majesty's officers.”

No. 5. 

A Catcutation, shewing at what time a ship must sail from England, and arrive in and depart 
from India, so as to perform Eight successive Voyages, without intermission, in the shortest 
possible time, 

THE data assumed for the Calculation are these = 

‘That three weeks be allowed for the receipt of the cargo outward. 

That if the ship sails from England in the favourable season of the year, her passage shall be 
considered to consume from four to five months, say, the mediuin of four months and a half; and 
in the unfavourable season, five months. 

‘That six:weeks be allowed for the landing of the Europe, and the receipt of the Indian cargo. 

That if she is dispatched home inthe unfavourable season of the year, her passaze be con- 
sidered the same as in the voyage outward, at five months; or in the favourable season, four 
months and a half, 

That three weeks be allowed for the delivery of the cargo homeward ; and, 

That one week be allowed for surveying, and making sny trifling repairs she may be found to 
stand in need of, previous to her departing upon an ensuing voyage.

HE Chairman, and Deputy Chairman, of the Court of Directors of the Eaft India 
Company, have been pleated to communicate to your honourable Committee avery” 
elaborate and detailed Paper, intituled “ Objervations on the Evidence given before the Com- 
“ mittee: of the Houfe of Commous, appointed for the Conjideration of India Affairs, on 
“ the Suljeét of the Private Trade with India” The title of this work does not futticiently 
detpeak e extent and variety of difeuilion which it embraces; for it is addreiled rather to 
the (serie object of the enquiry, in which the honourable Committee is engaged, than 
confined to the particular branch to which the evidence it comments upon, was directed. 
The’ Authors of the following Remarks, however, do not ba the By of explaining 
or elucidating-the topics. on which they were examined. ey truft that the candour of your
